detail:
NICHD describes endometriosis care as focused on pain, infertility, and a person's pregnancy goals, noting there is no cure and treatment is chosen with a health care provider. For milder symptoms, pain medicines are described, ranging from over-the-counter relievers to stronger prescription options a clinician may consider. Care also involves follow-up on pain, fertility plans, and effects on daily life, since relief from any single approach can be temporary.

Hormone therapy is a main approach NICHD describes for endometriosis-associated pain. Options listed include gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) medicines, including the oral medicine elagolix, oral contraceptives that can make periods lighter and more regular, and progesterone and progestin given by pill, injection, or intrauterine device. Surgical treatments described include laparoscopy to view and remove growths and, in more extensive cases, laparotomy. For infertility related to endometriosis, assisted reproduction such as IVF is described as an option clinicians may discuss.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing endometriosis pain and fertility.
sourceName: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
sourceVideoTitle: What are the treatments for endometriosis?
summary: NICHD describes endometriosis treatments for pain as including pain medicines, hormone therapies such as GnRH medicines, oral contraceptives, and progestins, and surgical treatments including laparoscopy.
takeaways: there is no cure described; treatment focuses on pain and fertility goals
hormone therapies are a main class clinicians describe for pain
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
surgery is described for severe pain or when other treatment does not help
title: Managing endometriosis day to day
